## First Apartment Essentials Checklist (Canada, Real Prices)

URL: https://smallspacehome.ca/blog/first-apartment-essentials-checklist-canada/

Moving into a first apartment in Canada means figuring out what you actually need versus what every "essentials list" online tells you to buy. Most of those lists are written for American readers, priced in USD, and assume you have a car to haul everything home from Target — which doesn't exist here.

This checklist is specifically for Canadian renters. Real CAD prices, Canadian stores (IKEA, Canadian Tire, Amazon.ca, Dollarama, Facebook Marketplace), and a priority order that puts daily essentials before furniture and decor.

> **Key Takeaways**
> - Buy in priority order: sleep → bathroom → kitchen → cleaning → furniture → decor.
> - A functional first apartment costs roughly $1,500–$2,500 CAD new, or $800–$1,400 CAD mixing secondhand.
> - Facebook Marketplace saves 40–60% on furniture in most Canadian cities.
> - Skip the coffee table, TV stand, and full dining set — add those once you know how the space works.

**TL;DR:** Sleep setup first (mattress + pillow + sheets, ~$350–$550 CAD), then bathroom basics (~$40 CAD), kitchen essentials (~$60 CAD), and cleaning supplies (~$25 CAD). That's ~$475–$675 CAD to be fully functional on day one. Furniture and decor come after.

---

## The Priority Order: What to Buy First

Most first-apartment mistakes happen because people buy furniture and decor before solving the basics. A sofa looks nice, but you can sit on the floor for a week — you can't sleep without a mattress or cook without a pan.

**The order that works:**
1. Sleep setup
2. Bathroom basics
3. Kitchen essentials
4. Cleaning supplies
5. Furniture (sofa, table, storage)
6. Decor and styling

Follow this sequence and you'll never be stuck in an apartment with a nice rug but no towels.

## 1. Sleep Setup (~$350–$550 CAD)

The mattress is the single most expensive purchase and the one most worth spending on. You'll spend a third of your life on it, and a bad mattress wrecks everything else — energy, mood, productivity.

| Item | Cost (CAD) | Where |
|------|-----------|-------|
| Mattress (queen, boxed) | $250–$400 | Amazon.ca, IKEA, Walmart |
| Pillow (2-pack) | $25–$40 | Amazon.ca, IKEA |
| Sheet set (queen) | $30–$50 | IKEA, Walmart |
| Duvet + cover | $50–$80 | IKEA |
| **Total** | **$355–$570** | |

**Canadian-specific tip:** IKEA Canada's VESTERÖY mattress (~$349 CAD for a queen) is the best-value boxed mattress available in-store. Amazon.ca bed-in-a-box options (Zinus, Linenspa) start around $250 CAD. Skip the bed frame for now — the mattress goes on the floor until you find a frame on Facebook Marketplace for $50–$100 CAD.

For long-term bedroom storage, a bed frame with built-in drawers (IKEA NORDLI, $399–$699 CAD) replaces the need for a dresser entirely — see our [small bedroom storage guide](/blog/small-apartment-bedroom-storage-ideas) for the full system.

![A clean, minimal bedroom setup in a small Canadian apartment](/images/bedroom-minimalist.jpg)

## 2. Bathroom Basics (~$40–$70 CAD)

You need these on day one — before you unpack a single box, you'll want to shower.

| Item | Cost (CAD) | Where |
|------|-----------|-------|
| Bath towels (2) | $15–$25 | IKEA, Walmart |
| Bath mat | $10–$15 | Walmart, Dollarama |
| Shower curtain + rings | $10–$20 | Dollarama, IKEA |
| Toilet brush + plunger | $8–$12 | Dollarama, Canadian Tire |
| **Total** | **$43–$72** | |

**Skip for now:** a bathroom organizer, matching towel sets, bath accessories. Get the basics working first. When you're ready to organize the bathroom properly, our [small apartment bathroom storage guide](/blog/bathroom-storage-small-apartment-canada) covers the full vertical storage system for under $180 CAD.

## 3. Kitchen Essentials (~$60–$120 CAD)

You don't need a full kitchen setup on day one. You need to be able to boil water, cook a basic meal, and eat it.

| Item | Cost (CAD) | Where |
|------|-----------|-------|
| Electric kettle | $15–$25 | Canadian Tire, Amazon.ca |
| Frying pan (non-stick, 10") | $15–$25 | Canadian Tire, IKEA |
| Pot with lid | $15–$20 | Canadian Tire, IKEA |
| Cutting board + knife | $10–$15 | Dollarama, IKEA |
| Plates (4), bowls (4), mugs (4) | $10–$20 | Dollarama, IKEA |
| Cutlery set (4-place) | $8–$12 | Dollarama, IKEA |
| Dish rack | $5–$10 | Dollarama |
| **Total** | **$78–$127** | |

**Skip for now:** a toaster, blender, microwave (check if your apartment includes one — most Canadian rentals do), specialty gadgets, a full knife set. Add those once you've cooked in the space for a month and know what you actually use.

Once the kitchen is functional, [small space kitchen organization](/blog/small-space-kitchen-organization) covers the zone-based system that keeps a tiny kitchen workable, and [fridge and pantry organization](/blog/small-space-kitchen-organization) handles the food storage side.

## 4. Cleaning Supplies (~$25–$40 CAD)

Your landlord will inspect at move-out. Start clean, stay clean — it protects your damage deposit.

| Item | Cost (CAD) | Where |
|------|-----------|-------|
| All-purpose cleaner | $4–$6 | Dollarama, Canadian Tire |
| Broom + dustpan | $8–$12 | Dollarama, Canadian Tire |
| Garbage bags (box) | $4–$6 | Dollarama |
| Dish soap + sponges | $3–$5 | Dollarama |
| Paper towels (2-pack) | $4–$6 | Dollarama, Walmart |
| Laundry detergent | $6–$10 | Walmart, Dollarama |
| **Total** | **$29–$45** | |

**Canadian-specific:** Dollarama is the single best store for cleaning supplies in Canada — nearly everything on this list is $1.50–$5 CAD there. Don't overspend at Canadian Tire or Walmart on cleaning products you'll use up in a month anyway.

## 5. Furniture — Buy Slowly (~$500–$1,200 CAD)

This is where most first-apartment renters overspend. The rule: buy only what you need *this week*, not what you think the apartment should eventually have.

### Week 1 — the essentials

| Item | Cost (CAD) | Where |
|------|-----------|-------|
| Small desk or table | $50–$100 | IKEA, Facebook Marketplace |
| Desk chair or dining chair (1–2) | $30–$80 | IKEA, Facebook Marketplace |
| Floor lamp | $35–$50 | IKEA, Amazon.ca |
| Hangers (50-pack velvet) | $18 | Amazon.ca |
| **Total** | **$133–$248** | |

### Week 2–4 — add as needed

| Item | Cost (CAD) | Where |
|------|-----------|-------|
| Sofa or loveseat | $300–$600 | Facebook Marketplace, IKEA |
| Bed frame | $50–$200 | Facebook Marketplace, IKEA |
| Small dresser or KALLAX | $79–$150 | IKEA, Facebook Marketplace |
| **Total** | **$429–$950** | |

**The Facebook Marketplace rule:** Check Marketplace before buying anything new that costs over $50 CAD. In Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal, Ottawa, and Calgary, quality secondhand furniture regularly lists at 40–60% off retail — especially during university move-out season in April and August. Our [Facebook Marketplace furniture guide](/blog/facebook-marketplace-furniture-guide-canada) covers what to search, red flags to avoid, and pickup safety.

For choosing the right furniture sizes, [small space furniture](/blog/small-space-furniture) covers the measurements that actually matter in a Canadian apartment — the pieces that fit through standard apartment doorways and don't overwhelm a 500 sq ft space.

![A well-furnished small apartment with secondhand and IKEA furniture](/images/eclectic-vintage-apartment-furniture.jpg)

## 6. Decor — Last, Not First (~$50–$200 CAD)

Decor is the fun part, but it's the last priority. An apartment with good lighting and clear surfaces looks better than one with art on every wall and clutter on every shelf.

**The only day-one decor purchase:** warm 2700K LED bulbs (~$15 CAD for a 4-pack at Canadian Tire). Swap every bulb in the apartment — it transforms how the whole space feels in five minutes.

Everything else — rugs, art, plants, cushions — can wait. When you're ready, follow the priority order in our [budget apartment decor guide](/blog/storage-ideas-for-small-places), which covers both $50 and $200 CAD tiers, or go the dollar-store route with [Dollarama finds that actually look expensive](/blog/dollarama-finds-look-expensive).

## The Complete First Apartment Budget

| Category | Budget (CAD) | New | With Secondhand |
|----------|-------------|-----|----------------|
| Sleep setup | $355–$570 | $400 | $300 |
| Bathroom | $43–$72 | $55 | $55 |

A fully functional, comfortable first apartment in Canada for roughly $1,000–$1,500 CAD. Not showroom-ready — liveable, comfortable, and ready to improve gradually over the next few months.

## What to Skip Entirely (For Now)

These are the items every "essentials list" includes that first-apartment renters in Canada don't actually need on day one — or often at all:

- **Coffee table** — wait until you know your living room layout; most small apartments don't have room for one
- **TV stand** — the TV sits on the dresser, a shelf, or a $30 CAD wall mount
- **Full dining set** — a small 2-person table and two chairs is enough for a one-bedroom
- **Bookshelf** — IKEA KALLAX does double duty as storage and display for ~$79 CAD
- **Desk lamp** — the floor lamp covers the desk area too, in a small apartment
- **Matching anything** — coordinated sets look nice but cost 2–3x more than buying individual pieces that simply don't clash

## The Organization System (Once You're Settled)

After the first month, the apartment has stuff in it — and it's probably starting to feel cluttered. That's when organization matters.

The system is simple: declutter first, then give every item a home, then maintain with a 10-minute daily reset. Our [small apartment organization guide](/blog/storage-ideas-for-small-places) covers the full room-by-room system, and [storage ideas for small places](/blog/storage-ideas-for-small-places) covers the specific products (bins, baskets, shelves) that work best in Canadian apartments.

**The five highest-impact organization purchases for a first apartment:**

1. Slim velvet hangers, 50-pack (~$18 CAD) — [closet organization](/blog/small-closet-organization-rental-apartment)
2. IKEA SKUBB under-bed bags (~$14 CAD) — [under-bed storage](/blog/under-bed-storage-ideas-small-apartment)
3. Stackable clear pantry bins (~$5–$8 each) — [kitchen organization](/blog/small-space-kitchen-organization)
4. Command hooks, 4-pack (~$12 CAD) — [entryway storage](/blog/small-entryway-hallway-storage-ideas)
5. Over-door organizer (~$28–$35 CAD) — [bedroom storage](/blog/small-apartment-bedroom-storage-ideas)

Total: ~$77–$93 CAD for an organization foundation that covers every room.

## The 30-Day First Apartment Timeline

**Day 1:** Sleep setup + bathroom basics + cleaning supplies. You can sleep, shower, and clean.

**Day 2–3:** Kitchen essentials. You can cook.

**Week 1:** Swap light bulbs. Add a floor lamp. Buy hangers and unpack clothes.

**Week 2:** First furniture — a small table and chair, or a desk if you work from home (see our [small apartment home office guide](/blog/small-apartment-home-office-ideas)).

**Week 3–4:** Add the sofa and any remaining furniture. Check Facebook Marketplace before buying new.

**Month 2:** Start the [organization system](/blog/storage-ideas-for-small-places). For the decor layer, [Dollarama finds that actually look expensive](/blog/dollarama-finds-look-expensive) is the fastest way to style surfaces for under $60 CAD.

The apartment doesn't need to be finished in a weekend. It needs to be liveable on day one, comfortable by week two, and organized by month two. Everything else is gradual.

## Floating Shelves: Renter-Friendly Options in Canada

URL: https://smallspacehome.ca/blog/floating-shelves-apartment-canada/

Floating shelves are one of the most searched storage upgrades for small apartments — and for good reason. A wall shelf adds display and storage space without touching the floor, which is exactly what small-space living needs. The problem for Canadian renters is the wall. Landlords own it, damage deposits are real, and most leases in Ontario, BC, and Quebec restrict permanent modifications.

This guide covers every method that works in a rental apartment, from truly no-damage options to proper drilling for tenants whose leases allow it.

---

## The Four Options for Floating Shelves in a Rental

Before buying anything, know which method your situation allows:

**1. Adhesive shelves** — no drilling, removable if done correctly, limited to light loads (2–5 kg). Best for small decorative shelves, spice racks, or display items.

**2. Tension pole shelves** — pole presses between floor and ceiling, shelves clip to the pole. Zero wall contact, holds 15–30 kg per pole depending on the model. Good for kitchen corners, home office zones, and anywhere you need real storage capacity.

**3. Freestanding ladder shelves** — leans against the wall, no mounting at all. Floor space cost is minimal (30–40 cm deep), holds significant weight, fully portable. Not technically a floating shelf, but achieves a very similar visual effect.

**4. Drilled installation** — proper studs or toggle bolts, holds everything, looks the best, requires permission or willingness to patch. Standard for condo owners; possible for some renters with landlord agreement.

Most Canadian renters should combine methods: adhesive for spice shelves and small bathroom storage, freestanding for main living area display, drilled for a home office or primary shelving wall if the landlord allows it.

---

## Adhesive Floating Shelves: What Actually Works

Adhesive shelving is sold widely in Canada — Canadian Tire, IKEA, Amazon.ca — but performance varies dramatically by product and wall condition.

### Products that work

**Command Picture Ledge Strips** (3M brand, available at Canadian Tire ~$12–$18): Designed for small ledge shelves up to 2.3 kg loaded. Use on smooth, flat, painted drywall only. Not for textured walls, wallpaper, or brick.

**Command Large Strips (White or Clear)**: Each pair holds 3.6 kg. A shelf needing 4 strips can theoretically hold 7 kg, but 3M advises against combining more than 4 strips — too many points of flex. Practical limit: 4–5 kg per shelf.

**IKEA SKÅDIS pegboard**: Technically not a shelf, but mounts to the wall with 4 screws into drywall and holds accessories up to 10 kg total. Removable holes patch with standard spackle. Very popular for home office, kitchen, and entryway use.

### Walls that work (and walls that don't)

Adhesive works best on:
- **Flat, smooth, painted drywall** — standard in most Canadian apartment buildings built after 1990
- **Painted concrete** — less common in residential, but common in loft and industrial apartments; adhesion is good if the paint is sound

Adhesive does NOT work reliably on:
- **Textured or orange-peel walls** — contact surface is too uneven
- **Recently painted walls (under 7 days)** — paint needs to cure before adhesive bonds properly
- **Oil-painted or gloss walls** — poor adhesion
- **Wallpaper** — strips pull the paper off, not just the adhesive

**Removal tip**: Always pull strips parallel to the wall surface (straight down for vertical strips), not at an angle. The stretch-release tab on Command strips is designed to prevent drywall damage when used correctly. Do it slowly — two to three minutes per strip.

---

## Tension Pole Shelves: The Best No-Damage Option for Real Storage

If you need a shelf that holds actual weight — books, kitchen gear, a printer, baskets of clothing — tension pole shelves are the answer. They press between floor and ceiling with spring or screw tension and carry their weight through the structure of the pole, not the wall.

### What to buy in Canada

**SUPERJARE 5-Tier Tension Shelf** (~$60–$80 on Amazon.ca): Fits ceilings 220–295 cm, holds about 25 kg total across 5 shelves. Available in black and white finishes.

**SONGMICS Tension Pole Shelf** (~$70–$90): Very popular with Canadians for bathrooms and laundry closets. 4-shelf version fits standard Canadian 8-foot ceilings (243 cm).

**WENKO Turbo-LOC Series**: Available at Walmart Canada and Amazon.ca (~$45–$65). The tension mechanism is tighter than most competitors and holds well on uneven tile ceilings.

### Best uses in a Canadian apartment

- **Kitchen corner**: A tension pole in the corner of a small kitchen adds spice, oil, and dry goods storage without touching the backsplash or cabinets
- **Bathroom**: Over the toilet or in the shower corner, where wall damage from humidity is a real risk even with proper screws
- **Home office nook**: A pole with 4–5 shelves in a corner holds printer, binders, reference materials, and monitor accessories without a desk return or wall unit
- **Laundry closet**: A pole in the back corner holds detergent, dryer sheets, and cleaning supplies vertically

---

## Freestanding Ladder Shelves: Zero Installation Required

A ladder shelf leans against the wall at a slight angle. Nothing attaches to the wall. It holds 30–50 kg on most designs, costs $60–$180 CAD, and moves with you.

The visual effect is close to wall-mounted shelving — shelves appear to float at different heights — but the base sits on the floor. In a room with good vertical space, a ladder shelf draws the eye upward and adds significant storage.

### Canadian options

**IKEA ENHET** (~$90): A wall unit that also works freestanding with the right feet kit. Very modular — add or remove shelves and doors.

**IKEA LERBERG** (~$50): Bare ladder shelf, industrial/metal look, fits small corners well. Light (8 kg), so it tips if loaded unevenly — place heavier items on the lower rungs.

**Amazon Basics 5-Shelf Bookcase** (~$70): Wide, stable base, available at Amazon.ca with fast shipping. Neutral finish works in most apartment aesthetics. For wall-mounted floating shelves specifically, this [Love-KANKEI solid wood set of 3](https://www.amazon.ca/dp/B077GQ87NP?tag=smallspace06f-20) (~$25–$35 CAD) is the most-reviewed option on Amazon.ca Canada — 51,000+ ratings, solid wood with metal bracket.

**Winners / HomeSense**: Carry solid wood and bamboo ladder shelf styles seasonally, typically $80–$150. Worth checking before buying online — quality variation is high, so seeing it in person matters.

### What makes a freestanding ladder shelf stable

- **Base width**: Wider base = more stable. For a 5-shelf unit, base width should be at least 60 cm
- **Wall lean angle**: The shelf should lean at roughly 75–80 degrees (nearly vertical). Shallower angles increase tipping risk
- **Load balance**: Heaviest items go on the bottom two shelves, lighter decorative items at the top
- **Non-slip feet**: Most good units come with felt or rubber feet. If yours doesn't, furniture foot pads from Canadian Tire (~$5) solve the sliding problem on hardwood

---

## Proper Drilled Installation (If Your Lease Allows It)

For renters who have permission, or condo owners, drilled floating shelves are far more secure and look cleaner than any no-damage option.

### Find studs first

Studs in Canadian residential construction are typically 16 inches (40.6 cm) apart, occasionally 24 inches (61 cm) in older buildings. A magnetic stud finder (Canadian Tire, ~$10–$20) detects the drywall screws used to attach drywall to studs.

Into a stud, a 3-inch wood screw holds 50+ kg. Into drywall only, a standard screw holds about 5 kg and will eventually tear out.

### When there's no stud where you want it

Use **toggle bolts** (also called butterfly anchors or Molly bolts). They unfold inside the wall cavity and spread the load against the back of the drywall. A single 3/8-inch toggle bolt holds 15–25 kg in standard 12.7 mm drywall.

Steps:
1. Drill a hole sized to the toggle's folded width (usually 12–14 mm for a standard toggle bolt)
2. Fold the toggle flat, insert through the hole, then tighten — the wings open inside the wall
3. Hold the bolt in position while tightening to prevent spin

Toggle bolts leave a 12–14 mm hole when removed, which patches with standard spackle and touch-up paint. Most landlords accept this if disclosed at move-out.

### Bracket style vs. French cleat

**Bracket shelves** (shelf rests on L-shaped metal or wood bracket): Easier to install, straightforward weight distribution, visible bracket. Good for heavy shelves with rustic or industrial aesthetics.

**French cleat** (angled wall-mount strip, shelf hangs on it): Allows infinite shelf repositioning, distributes weight across the full cleat length, completely adjustable. Ideal for gallery walls or home office setups with multiple shelves at different heights. Requires a long, flat, level mount — better suited to stud installation.

**Invisible bracket / hidden pin mount** (shelf slides onto pins embedded in the wall): Cleanest look, the shelf appears to float with no hardware visible. More complex installation — pins must be precisely aligned with pre-drilled holes in the shelf back. Most pre-made floating shelves from IKEA (BERGSHULT/GRANHULT system) and Amazon use this method.

---

## Floating Shelf Ideas by Room

### Living room

A 100–120 cm floating shelf above the sofa works as a photo display, plant ledge, or book storage. Keep it light — 3–5 items maximum — to avoid the cluttered look. Position it at roughly 165–175 cm from the floor (eye level when standing, comfortable to reach).

For a full gallery wall effect without full installation: a ladder shelf in the corner behind the sofa with a mix of books, plants, and framed prints achieves a very similar look at zero wall damage.

### Kitchen

The most impactful kitchen upgrade in a small Canadian apartment is a floating spice shelf above or beside the stove. A 60 cm adhesive ledge shelf holds 12–15 standard spice jars (each weighs 100–200 g — well within Command strip capacity). This frees up an entire cabinet.

Open shelving to replace upper cabinet doors is not renter-friendly (you'd have to reinstall the doors at move-out). But adding a shelf above the existing cabinets or between the counter and the cabinet bottom works without any modification.

### Bathroom

Over-toilet tension shelves and adhesive shelves above the mirror or beside the sink are the two standard solutions in small Canadian bathrooms. Adhesive works better in bathrooms than most renters expect — if the wall is smooth painted drywall (not tile), Command strips hold well in normal bathroom humidity. Avoid mounting directly above a shower or tub.

### Bedroom

A small floating shelf beside the bed replaces a nightstand and frees up floor space. Adhesive works at this scale (nightstand shelf typically holds a lamp, phone, water glass — 2–3 kg total). A shelf above the desk for books and supplies is the most common home office improvement in small apartments.

---

|---|---|---|---|

## Fridge Organization: How to Set It Up Right

URL: https://smallspacehome.ca/blog/fridge-organization-apartment-canada/

A disorganised fridge wastes food and money. In a small Canadian apartment where the fridge itself may be compact (bar fridge, apartment-size 10–14 cubic foot, or a full-size shared with a roommate), the problem is amplified — items get pushed to the back, forgotten, and thrown out. The average Canadian household wastes approximately $1,300 in food per year, and a significant portion of that is fridge-related spoilage.

The fix is a zone system, not more containers. Containers help, but buying bins before establishing zones just means organised chaos.

---

## Step 1: Clear and Clean

Remove everything from the fridge. Check every item:

- Expired? Discard
- Condiment with less than one use left? Use it tonight or discard
- Mystery container from two weeks ago? Discard
- Duplicate items (three open jars of the same thing)? Consolidate

This step alone typically frees 20–30% of fridge space. Wipe every shelf and drawer liner before putting anything back.

---

## Step 2: The Zone System

### Top shelf — ready to eat

Leftovers, cooked food, deli meats, drinks, yogurt, and anything that needs no further preparation before eating. This shelf should be the most visible and easiest to reach — if something is ready to eat, it should be the first thing you see when you open the door. This reduces the "I don't know what to eat" problem that leads to ordering takeout when the fridge is actually full.

**Temperature note:** The top shelf is the warmest part of the fridge (warm air rises). Cooked leftovers and prepared foods are fine here. Raw meat should not go here.

### Middle shelf — dairy and eggs

Milk, cheese, butter, and eggs stay at consistent mid-fridge temperature. Eggs do not need a special egg holder — the standard egg carton is fine and takes less space than a fixed egg tray.

### Bottom shelf — raw meat and fish

The coldest shelf in the fridge. Raw meat and fish go here, sealed in their original packaging or in a sealed container, placed on a small plate or tray to catch any drips. This prevents cross-contamination with everything below.

### Crisper drawers — produce separated

Most apartment fridges have two crisper drawers. Use one for high-humidity produce (leafy greens, broccoli, herbs, cucumber) and one for low-humidity produce (apples, pears, grapes, berries). Check the drawer settings — most have a sliding vent. High humidity = vent closed; low humidity = vent open.

**Do not mix:** Fruits that produce ethylene gas (apples, pears, stone fruits) accelerate ripening in nearby vegetables. Keep them in separate drawers or at least away from leafy greens.

### Door — condiments and drinks only

The door is the warmest, most temperature-variable part of the fridge (it opens and closes constantly). Condiments, juices, water, and high-acid items (ketchup, mustard, hot sauce, salad dressing) belong here. Milk and eggs should never be stored in the door — the temperature fluctuation shortens their shelf life significantly.

---

## Step 3: Clear Bins and Containers

Once the zones are established, bins prevent the "lost at the back of the shelf" problem.

### What bins to use

**[Clear stackable fridge bins](https://www.amazon.ca/dp/B014Q8AZRO?tag=smallspace06f-20)** (~$5–$10 each at Amazon.ca): Group similar items — one bin for cheese and deli items, one for snacks and grab-and-go items, one for small condiment jars that don't fit in the door. Slide the bin out to access the back rather than moving individual items.

**Lazy Susan (turntable)** (~$10–$15, Amazon.ca or Canadian Tire): Place in the back corner of the top or middle shelf for condiments, sauces, and small jars. Spin to access anything without reaching.

**Produce wash-and-store containers** (~$8–$15 each): Containers with a colander insert — wash produce, drain, store in the container. Berries last 2–3× longer in these than in their original plastic clamshells. The colander keeps moisture from pooling at the bottom.

**Can dispenser** (~$10–$20, Amazon.ca): A gravity-feed rack that holds canned drinks, loading from the back and dispensing from the front. In a small apartment fridge shared between two people, this keeps cans organised and prevents a fridge full of randomly placed cans.

### What to decant and what not to

**Worth decanting:**
- Leftovers from pots and pans → clear square containers (square containers pack more efficiently than round)
- Bulk items (a large bag of shredded cheese) → a smaller sealed container
- Fresh herbs → a small jar with water (like a bouquet), covered loosely with a bag

**Not worth decanting:**
- Original packaging that seals well (yogurt tubs, deli containers, cheese packages with resealable zip)
- Small items that will be used within 2 days

---

## What Does Not Belong in a Small Fridge

Removing non-essential items from a small apartment fridge makes a meaningful difference:

| Item | Where it actually belongs |
|---|---|
| Whole tomatoes | Counter (room temperature) |
| Potatoes and sweet potatoes | Cool dark cupboard |
| Onions and garlic | Mesh bag in a cool cupboard |
| Bread | Counter in a bread box or bag, or freezer |
| Hot sauce, soy sauce, ketchup | Cupboard (after opening — fine for months) |
| Honey | Cupboard indefinitely |
| Most cooking oils | Cupboard (except nut oils — those do go in the fridge) |
| Avocados (unripened) | Counter until ripe, then fridge |

Clearing these items can free up an entire shelf in a compact apartment fridge.

---

## Canadian Products for Fridge Organization

| Product | Where | Price CAD |
|---|---|---|
| Clear stackable fridge bins (set of 4) | Amazon.ca | $20–$35 |
| Lazy Susan turntable (25 cm) | Amazon.ca, Canadian Tire | $12–$20 |
| Produce wash-and-store containers | Amazon.ca, Winners | $8–$15 each |
| Can dispenser rack | Amazon.ca | $10–$20 |
| Egg holder (holds 14) | Amazon.ca | $8–$15 |
| Fridge deodorizer (baking soda style) | Canadian Tire, Walmart Canada | $4–$8 |

A full fridge organization kit — 4 bins, a lazy Susan, and produce containers — runs $40–$65 at Amazon.ca. Most people find they need only 3–4 bins to transform the shelf organisation.

For kitchen storage beyond the fridge, [small space kitchen organization](/blog/small-space-kitchen-organization) covers cabinets, counters, and pantry in a small Canadian apartment kitchen. If you're tackling a broader apartment organisation project, our guide to [storage ideas for small places](/blog/storage-ideas-for-small-places) covers every room.

## Hallway Storage Ideas for Narrow Corridors

URL: https://smallspacehome.ca/blog/hallway-storage-small-apartment-canada/

Most Canadian apartment hallways present the same problem: too narrow for standard furniture, no natural light, and no obvious place to put anything. A typical apartment corridor is 90–110 cm wide — enough to walk through comfortably but not enough for a normal shelving unit or console table without blocking the path.

The solutions are all about depth. Furniture and organizers that are 20–25 cm deep function in a hallway without compromising circulation. Everything wider than 30 cm starts to feel cramped.

---

## The Depth Rule

Before buying anything for an apartment hallway, measure the width of the narrowest point of the corridor. Subtract 75 cm for clear walking width (the minimum comfortable path for one person). The remainder is your maximum furniture depth.

| Hallway width | Max furniture depth |
|---|---|
| 90 cm | 15 cm |
| 100 cm | 25 cm |
| 110 cm | 35 cm |
| 120 cm+ | 45 cm |

A 90 cm hallway (common in older Canadian apartment buildings) can only accommodate wall-mounted items, floating shelves, and hooks — no freestanding furniture. A 110 cm hallway fits a slim console table. A 120 cm+ hallway (less common in rental apartments) can accommodate a narrow cabinet.

---

## Solution 1: Floating Wall Shelves

A floating shelf at 180–190 cm height above the hallway floor holds items that pass in and out regularly: bags, seasonal hats and gloves, a spare umbrella. At this height, the shelf does not interfere with head clearance (standard Canadian apartment ceiling is 240–260 cm) and adds storage without touching the floor zone at all.

**Depth:** 15–20 cm is sufficient for a hallway display shelf. Deep enough for bags and accessories; shallow enough to not reduce the perceived width of the corridor.

**What to store:** Bags in active rotation, a spare set of keys, seasonal accessories (winter scarves and gloves near the door for easy grab on the way out), mail that needs to be dealt with.

**Installation:** Two screws per bracket. For a narrow hallway where every wall matters, toggle bolts into drywall are fine for items under 10 kg total. See [wall mounted shelves guide](/blog/wall-mounted-shelves-apartment-canada) for full installation detail.

**Cost:** $20–$50 for a shelf and brackets at IKEA or Amazon.ca.

---

## Solution 2: Slim Console Table (100 cm hallways or wider)

A slim console table at 25–30 cm depth fits in a hallway without blocking circulation when the corridor is 100 cm or wider. It provides a surface for keys, mail, and small items — and can hold a small drawer unit underneath for more organized storage.

**What to put on it:** A key bowl or hook for keys, a small tray for daily-carry items (transit card, lip balm, earbuds), a plant or small lamp to make the hallway feel like a transition zone rather than just a corridor.

**What to put underneath:** A small basket for shoes, a slim recycling bag, or a door mat. Not a large shoe rack — the floor under a console table in a narrow hallway is not a high-volume storage zone.

**Canadian options:**
- **IKEA LUNNARP** (~$100, 26 cm deep): Slim bamboo console, fits most Canadian apartment hallways
- **Amazon.ca slim console tables** (~$60–$120): Wide variety of finishes, most in the 25–30 cm depth range. Look for one with a drawer for the key-and-mail zone.
- **HomeSense / Winners** (~$80–$150): Good selection of solid wood slim tables seasonally

---

## Solution 3: Hooks and a Mirror

The combination of a hook rail and a large mirror solves two problems at once: coat and bag storage, and the dark-narrow-hallway visual problem.

### Hook placement

Mount hooks at 165–175 cm height — accessible for adults without reaching overhead. A row of 4–5 hooks across a wall segment handles coats, bags, and umbrellas for a household of two.

**No-drill option:** Command Large hooks ($5–$8 each at Canadian Tire) hold up to 3.6 kg each. A coat on a hanger weighs 0.5–1.5 kg — well within capacity. For heavier items (winter parkas, large bags), use screwed hooks — a parka can exceed 3 kg.

### Mirror placement

A full-length leaner mirror (100 cm+ tall) at the end of the hallway or on a side wall reflects the corridor length back on itself — the hallway reads as longer than it is. In a dark hallway, the mirror also bounces any available light (from a window at the corridor end, or from the rooms on either side) back through the space.

**No-installation option:** A leaner mirror sits against the wall with no mounting. Best at the end of the corridor or angled in a corner.

**Cost:** IKEA NISSEDAL mirror (~$80), or leaner mirrors at HomeSense (~$60–$150).

---

## Solution 4: Over-Door Organizers

The back of a door in or near the hallway — a coat closet door, a bathroom door, a linen closet door — is available storage that most apartment renters ignore.

An over-door organizer with pockets holds:
- Umbrellas (one large pocket each)
- Reusable shopping bags (folded)
- Hats and scarves
- Small bags and pouches

The organizer hangs on the door with a hook set — no mounting, no damage. When the door opens, the organizer clears the frame. A pocket organizer with 6–8 large pockets ($20–$35 at Amazon.ca) fits most standard Canadian apartment doors.

---

## Solution 5: Vertical Cabinet (120 cm+ hallways)

A tall narrow cabinet (30–35 cm deep, 40–50 cm wide, 180 cm tall) provides the most storage volume of any hallway solution. Closed cabinet doors hide everything inside — the hallway stays visually clean even when the cabinet is full.

Use it for: coats on hooks inside the cabinet, shoes on a low shelf, sports equipment, umbrellas in a door-mounted holder, bags.

**Canadian options:**
- **IKEA STUVA** storage combination (~$150–$200): 60 cm wide × 30 cm deep, available with doors. Works in hallways wider than 120 cm.
- **IKEA HEMNES shoe cabinet with drawers** (~$250): 89 cm wide, 30 cm deep, specifically designed for entryway use.
- **Wayfair Canada tall hallway cabinets** (~$150–$350): Various widths from 35–60 cm, door options, often with a mirror on the front.

---

## Hallway Lighting

A dark hallway with a single overhead fixture is both uninviting and practically dim. Two improvements that work without an electrician:

**Plug-in wall sconce:** A plug-in lamp with a cord that runs to the nearest outlet. The cord hides against the wall with cable clips ($3–$5 at Canadian Tire). Adds warm ambient light at eye level. IKEA carries plug-in wall lamps from $20–$60.

**LED motion sensor light:** A battery-powered LED strip or puck light mounted under a shelf or inside a cabinet activates when someone enters the hallway. No wiring, no switching on manually. Amazon.ca, ~$10–$25 for a 2-pack.

---

## Full Hallway Setup by Width

| Hallway width | Best setup |
|---|---|
| Under 90 cm | Hooks only + floating shelf at 185 cm + mirror |
| 90–100 cm | Hooks + floating shelf + over-door organizer on nearby door |
| 100–110 cm | Hooks + slim console table (25 cm deep) + mirror |
| 110–120 cm | All of the above + small bench or shoe rack beside table |
| 120 cm+ | Narrow tall cabinet + hooks + mirror |

For the specific entryway zone right at the front door, [entryway storage for small apartments](/blog/entryway-storage-small-apartment-canada) covers hooks, key storage, and shoe containment in detail. And for shoe storage that extends from the entryway into the bedroom closet, [shoe storage for small apartments](/blog/shoe-storage-small-apartment-canada) covers the full system.


---

## 15 IKEA Small Space Hacks for Apartments

URL: https://smallspacehome.ca/blog/ikea-small-space-hacks/

> **Start here:** The KALLAX 2×4 (~$159 CAD) is the single most versatile IKEA piece for a small apartment — room divider, TV console, entry bench, or wardrobe base. If you buy one thing from this list, buy the KALLAX.

The best IKEA hacks for small apartments use KALLAX as a room divider or entry bench, PAX to fix a weak closet, a NORDLI storage bed instead of a dresser, and BILLY or LACK pieces for height and floating storage, all without a drill.

IKEA is the default furniture store for Canadian apartment renters for good reason — it's designed for small spaces, available across Canada, and priced for people who might move in two years. But not everything works in a small apartment. These 15 ideas use IKEA products in smart configurations that solve real problems, with no cutting, no major modifications, and no need for a drill. CMHC data shows that rental affordability is a persistent challenge across Canadian cities, which makes budget-conscious furniture choices more important than ever.


> **In a hurry?** Buy the KALLAX — it's the most versatile piece at IKEA, working as a room divider, entryway bench, TV console, or home office. Then look at the NORDLI storage bed (replaces a dresser entirely), ceiling-height BILLY bookcases (maximum vertical storage in a 28 cm footprint), and LACK shelves on Command strips for floating nightstands that free floor space completely.

---

## How Do You Use KALLAX as a Room Divider in a Studio?

Place the KALLAX 2×4 vertically between the sleeping and living zones in a studio apartment. It creates a visual divider without blocking all the light, and both sides of the bookcase can be used for storage and display.

A KALLAX 2×4 unit costs about $159 CAD and, placed vertically between sleep and living zones, divides a studio without the light-blocking effect of a full wall.

Add plants on top of the divider to make the transition feel designed, not improvised. For more storage ideas across the rest of the apartment, see [storage ideas for small places](/blog/storage-ideas-for-small-places).

**Cost:** KALLAX 2×4 ~$159 CAD.

## Can a PAX Wardrobe Replace an Inadequate Closet?

Many older Toronto and Montreal apartments have tiny wardrobes or hall closets that don't function as a proper bedroom closet. A PAX wardrobe frame (50 cm deep, 201 cm tall) positioned against the bedroom wall creates a real wardrobe.

A PAX wardrobe frame starts around $179 CAD, but a full configuration with doors and interior organizers typically runs $400 to $800 CAD — still often cheaper than a custom closet build-out in an older Toronto or Montreal rental.

Add internal organizers: a [sliding wire pull-out basket](https://www.amazon.ca/dp/B000JF8LMK?tag=smallspace06f-20), JONAXEL shelf units, and a mirror door to make the bedroom feel significantly larger.

**Cost:** PAX frame starts at ~$179 CAD. Full configuration with doors and interior organizers: ~$400–$800 CAD.

## NORDLI Storage Bed to Eliminate the Dresser

The NORDLI bed frame has two large drawers on each side that hold as much as a full dresser — built into the bed itself. In a small bedroom, this removes the need for a separate dresser entirely and frees significant floor space.

A NORDLI Queen bed frame runs $399 to $699 CAD depending on configuration, but its built-in drawers hold as much as a full separate dresser, which is what actually frees up floor space in a small bedroom.

**Cost:** NORDLI Queen ~$399–$699 CAD depending on configuration.

## How Do You Take a BILLY Bookcase to the Ceiling?

The standard BILLY bookcase is 202 cm tall. Add the GNEDBY extension (40 cm) on top to take it to 242 cm — close to standard ceiling height. This gives you floor-to-ceiling storage in a 28 cm deep footprint.

Adding the $39 CAD GNEDBY extension takes a standard 202 cm BILLY bookcase to 242 cm, filling nearly the full ceiling height in a 28 cm deep footprint.

Anchor to the wall with the included anti-tip strap. In a rental, this requires one small screw in the wall — minimal damage and worth it for safety.

**Cost:** BILLY 80 cm wide ~$79–$99 CAD. GNEDBY extension ~$39 CAD.

![Floor-to-ceiling BILLY bookshelves maximize vertical storage in a small apartment](/images/blog-12-img2.jpg)

## Can a LACK Shelf Work as a Floating Nightstand?

The IKEA LACK shelf (30 × 26 cm, ~$15 CAD) is small enough to mount at nightstand height on Command strips, eliminating the floor footprint of a bedside table entirely. It holds a lamp, phone, water, and a book — everything a nightstand needs.

Two LACK shelves, one on each side of the bed, creates a symmetrical bedroom layout without consuming any floor space.

**Cost:** LACK small shelf ~$15 CAD. Command Large Strips ~$12–$15 CAD.

## Can KALLAX Double as Entryway Storage and a Bench?

Lay the 1×4 KALLAX horizontally at entry height (about 45 cm off the floor), top it with a $20–30 CAD bench cushion, and fill each cube with shoe and bag storage — it turns a $79 CAD bookcase into a functional mudroom-style entry bench. Add hooks on the wall above for coats.

This creates a proper mudroom-style entry in the smallest apartments.

**Cost:** KALLAX 1×4 ~$79 CAD. Bench pad or cushion ~$20–$30 CAD.

## Is RASKOG Worth It as a Kitchen or Bathroom Cart?

The RASKOG cart costs about $39 CAD and works as a rolling kitchen or bathroom cart, which matters most in apartments where a single room has to serve more than one purpose.

The RASKOG 3-tier cart (~$39 CAD) works beautifully as a kitchen cart that rolls out during cooking for extra counter space, then tucks away. In the bathroom it holds towels, toiletries, and a small plant — see [small apartment bathroom storage ideas](/blog/bathroom-storage-small-apartment-canada) for more no-drill options in the same price range. If you can't find the RASKOG in stock, Amazon.ca carries several nearly identical rolling carts at the same price point, and Wayfair Canada has a wider selection of kitchen carts if you want something with a more finished look.

In a small apartment where rooms serve multiple purposes, the rollability is actually the feature.

![A clean organized kitchen with smart storage — every inch used intentionally](/images/kitchen-organized-white.jpg)

## SKADIS Pegboard to Clear Counter Space

A SKADIS pegboard on the kitchen wall (or behind the desk) keeps tools and supplies accessible without consuming any counter or desk surface. It works with SKADIS-compatible hooks, containers, and clips.

A SKADIS pegboard costs about $15 CAD, and a basic accessory pack of hooks and containers adds another $5 to $15 CAD — enough to clear most loose tools off a kitchen or desk surface.

**Cost:** SKADIS 56 × 56 cm ~$15 CAD. Accessory pack (hooks + containers) ~$5–$15 CAD.

## How Do You Combine MICKE Desk and KALLAX for a Home Office?

KALLAX 2×2 placed beside the MICKE desk creates a corner [home office setup](/blog/small-apartment-home-office-ideas) with twice the storage. The KALLAX handles books, office supplies, and equipment that won't fit on the desk.

A MICKE desk paired with a 2×2 KALLAX totals about $178 CAD, doubling the storage of a desk-only setup in the same corner footprint.

**Cost:** MICKE desk ~$99 CAD. KALLAX 2×2 ~$79 CAD. Total: ~$178 CAD.

## IVAR Shelving Units as a Wardrobe System

The IVAR system is IKEA's most flexible storage system — it expands, reconfigures, and can be returned to a simple shelving unit if needed. In a bedroom, it creates a custom wardrobe system. In the kitchen or living room, it becomes a pantry or display unit.

IVAR sections start around $35 CAD each, with a full wardrobe configuration typically landing between $150 and $300 CAD — reconfigurable later if the room's needs change.

**Cost:** IVAR starting at ~$35 CAD per section. Full wardrobe configuration ~$150–$300 CAD.

## Does the HOVET Mirror Really Expand a Small Bedroom?

The [Umbra Bellwood leaning mirror](https://www.amazon.ca/dp/B0FF464B54?tag=smallspace06f-20) (~$225 CAD) leans against the wall (no installation) and immediately makes any small bedroom feel significantly larger. It reflects light from the window and creates the illusion of a second doorway.

The HOVET mirror costs about $279 CAD and needs no installation, since it simply leans against the wall while still creating the illusion of a second doorway.

## FRIHETEN as a Guest Bed for Studio Apartments

If you live in a studio and sometimes have overnight guests, the FRIHETEN sofa bed (~$999 CAD) solves both the "sofa" and "guest bed" problems in one piece. The storage chaise adds significant storage capacity.

The FRIHETEN sofa bed costs about $999 CAD, which is more than most single-purpose IKEA pieces on this list, but it replaces both a sofa and a guest bed in a studio apartment.

## How Does the SKUBB Under-Bed Storage System Work?

SKUBB [under-bed storage bags](/blog/under-bed-storage-ideas-small-apartment) (~$14 for 2) are flat, zip closed, and designed to slide under an IKEA bed frame. Store off-season clothing, extra bedding, or anything needed only twice a year.

SKUBB under-bed bags cost about $14 CAD for a pack of 2 and are the standard flat-storage option for anything only needed twice a year, like off-season clothing.

If combined with NORDLI or MALM bed risers, you can add even more under-bed clearance. If you'd rather skip the IKEA-specific bags, a similar [non-IKEA under-bed storage bag](https://amzn.to/4rwNiu6) from Amazon.ca does the same flat, zip-closed job.

![IKEA SKUBB under-bed storage bags are designed to slide under any IKEA bed frame](/images/blog-12-img4.jpg)

## TJUSIG Bench + Hooks as a Complete Entry System

The TJUSIG bench (~$59 CAD) with [shoe storage](/blog/small-entryway-hallway-storage-ideas) underneath, combined with TJUSIG or ENUDDEN wall hooks above (~$15–$25 CAD), creates a functional entry station for a fraction of a custom mudroom.

A TJUSIG bench costs about $59 CAD, and adding wall hooks for another $15 to $25 CAD creates a full entry station for well under $100 CAD total.

## Is JONAXEL Good as a Freestanding Wardrobe System?

The JONAXEL system is designed to stand freely without wall attachment — ideal for renters who can't drill. It functions as a full wardrobe: hanging space, shelves, and optional mesh bins.

A full JONAXEL wardrobe configuration runs $150 to $250 CAD depending on setup, and because it's freestanding, it works for renters who can't drill into walls at all.

**Cost:** JONAXEL frame + hanging rod + shelf ~$150–$250 CAD depending on configuration.

For a more specific look at budget-conscious organization, [small apartment organization ideas on a budget](/blog/storage-ideas-for-small-places) pairs well with this list — it covers what to buy first when you're starting from scratch.

## Linen Closet Organization for Small Apartments

URL: https://smallspacehome.ca/blog/linen-closet-organization-canada/

A linen closet in a small Canadian apartment is typically 60–90 cm wide, 40–50 cm deep, and 180–200 cm tall, with 3–4 fixed shelves. Most of them are full but barely functional — sheets fall out when you pull one set, towels are stacked too high to retrieve without everything shifting, and the bottom shelf holds a mix of things that have no other home.

The fix takes about 30 minutes and costs very little.

---

## Step 1: Edit the Contents

Remove everything. Sort into three piles:

**Keep:** Bedding and towels in regular rotation, cleaning supplies that belong here, medicines if this is the storage spot.

**Relocate:** Items that ended up here by default but belong elsewhere — tools, batteries, random small items, cleaning products for specific rooms.

**Discard:** Single pillowcases with no match, worn towels (downgrade to cleaning rags or discard), extra blankets that haven't been used in years, expired medicines.

Most people discard or relocate 20–30% of linen closet contents in this step. That freed space is more useful than any organizer.

---

## Step 2: Shelf Assignment by Category

Assign each shelf a single category. Mixed shelves — where towels share space with cleaning supplies and random items — mean nothing has a clear home and the closet returns to chaos within weeks.

**Top shelf (hardest to reach, 175–200 cm):**
Extra blankets, duvet inserts stored in their bags, seasonal items, rarely-used guest bedding. Keep in labelled bags or bins — items at this height are stored, not accessed regularly.

**Upper-middle shelf (eye level, ~140–165 cm):**
Bedding sets. One set per bed, stored as a unit using the pillowcase method (see FAQ above). If you have two beds, one half of the shelf per bed. This is the most-accessed shelf — it should have the clearest organisation.

**Lower-middle shelf (~100–130 cm):**
Towels. Stack towel sets together (bath towel + hand towel + face cloth) rather than all bath towels together then all hand towels. Retrieving a full set should be one motion. Roll towels instead of folding flat if the shelf is deep — rolled towels use less shelf depth and let you see everything without unstacking.

**Bottom shelf (floor level or lowest shelf):**
Cleaning supplies, extra toilet paper, medicines if stored here, or an overflow bin. Heavy items belong at the bottom — a full bottle of floor cleaner on a top shelf is a risk.

---

## Step 3: Add Storage Without Replacing Shelves

Most apartment linen closets have fixed shelves with 40–50 cm of vertical space between them — much more than a folded towel or sheet set needs. This gap is wasted unless you add a half-shelf organizer.

### Half-shelf organizer (stackable shelf insert)

A half-shelf insert sits on the existing shelf and creates a second level in the space above. A folded sheet set is typically 15–20 cm tall. A 40 cm gap between shelves means 20 cm of dead air above every stack. A half-shelf insert fills that gap.

**Cost:** $15–$30 at Amazon.ca. Expandable versions adjust to different shelf widths.

### Clear bins and baskets

Group small items in bins so they do not scatter when you retrieve something nearby. A small bin for face cloths, a bin for pillowcases, a bin for cleaning supplies — each bin pulls out as a unit.

**Cost:** $5–$12 per bin at Amazon.ca, HomeSense, or Dollarama. A [12-pack of foldable fabric organizer bins](https://www.amazon.ca/dp/B07X7F4YZN?tag=smallspace06f-20) (~$20–$25 CAD) covers an entire linen closet at once — 6 medium and 6 small bins that stack and fold flat when not in use.

### Labels

A label on each bin or zone eliminates the "just put it wherever" habit that undoes all organisation within a week. Peel-and-stick labels from a label maker (~$20–$30 at Canadian Tire for a basic Dymo model, labels included) or handwritten labels on masking tape are equally effective.

### Door back organizer

The back of the linen closet door (if hinged) holds an over-door organizer with pockets or hooks. Use it for:
- Spare medicine bottles
- Small cleaning tools (a lint roller, a stain remover stick)
- Extra toiletries
- Rarely-used but must-be-accessible items

**Cost:** $15–$30 at Amazon.ca.

---

## The Pillowcase Sheet-Folding Method

Fitted sheets are notoriously difficult to fold neatly. The pillowcase storage method solves this:

1. Lay the fitted sheet flat and tuck one corner into the other, forming a rough square
2. Fold in thirds to make a rectangle
3. Fold the flat sheet in thirds lengthwise, then into a rectangle matching the fitted sheet size
4. Stack: flat sheet, fitted sheet, then fold pillowcases into neat rectangles and place on top
5. Slide the whole stack inside one pillowcase
6. The pillowcase holds the complete set — place it on the shelf as one unit

Grabbing a full sheet change becomes one motion: take the pillowcase bundle, pull out the contents at the bed. Takes 3 minutes to fold a set once you have done it a few times.

---

## Towel Rolling vs. Folding

**Folded flat towels** stack efficiently on a deep shelf and look neat, but the stack height means you can only see the top towel — retrieving from the middle destabilises the pile.

**Rolled towels** stand vertically in a row on the shelf, letting you see every towel and retrieve any one without disturbing others. They use slightly more horizontal space per towel but significantly less vertical space — a 40 cm high shelf fits two rows of rolled towels (using ~30 cm of the height) vs. one neat stack of flat towels.

For a small linen closet, rolling works better on any shelf where you have multiple towels and want clear access without unstacking.

---

## Canadian Products for Linen Closet Organization

| Product | Where | Price CAD |
|---|---|---|
| Expandable half-shelf insert | Amazon.ca | $15–$30 |
| Clear stackable bins (set of 4) | Amazon.ca, HomeSense | $20–$35 |
| Over-door organizer (pockets) | Amazon.ca | $15–$25 |
| Label maker (Dymo basic) | Canadian Tire, Staples | $20–$30 |
| Vacuum storage bags (blankets) | Amazon.ca, Canadian Tire | $15–$30 for 6-pack |
| Shelf liner (non-slip) | Dollarama, Amazon.ca | $5–$10 |

A complete linen closet kit — half-shelf inserts, 4 bins, labels, and an over-door organizer — runs $60–$90 at Amazon.ca. Most people need only 2–3 of these items after the initial edit removes enough clutter to make the space workable.

For the bedroom closet that holds your clothing, [closet organization for small apartments](/blog/closet-organization-small-apartment-canada) covers the full system. And for bathroom storage that complements the linen closet, [bathroom storage for small apartments](/blog/bathroom-storage-small-apartment-canada) covers every bathroom zone.

## Noise Reduction Ideas for Canadian Apartments

URL: https://smallspacehome.ca/blog/noise-reduction-apartment-canada/

**TL;DR:** Soft surfaces (rugs, curtains, upholstered furniture) absorb sound inside your unit. Seal door and window gaps with removable weatherstripping to block hallway and street noise. Acoustic panels reduce echo but don't block wall-transmitted sound — for that, push a heavy bookshelf against the shared wall. White noise machines cover what you can't eliminate. All of this works without permanent changes or deposit risk.

Thin walls, hollow-core doors, and hard flooring are standard in Canadian apartment buildings. Whether you're in a Toronto high-rise, a Montreal walk-up, or a Vancouver concrete tower, the noise problem is usually the same: you hear too much of your neighbours, the hallway, and the street.

The good news is that most of the effective fixes are renter-friendly. They don't require drilling into walls, gluing anything permanent, or getting your landlord's written permission. If you're also working on how your apartment is arranged, our guide to [small apartment layout ideas](/blog/small-apartment-layout-ideas) covers furniture placement in more detail — and some of those layout changes help with noise too.

---

## Why Apartments Are Loud (and What You Can Actually Control)

Sound enters your apartment in two ways: **airborne noise** (voices, traffic, music) travels through air gaps around doors, windows, and vents. **Impact noise** (footsteps, dropped objects, furniture dragging) travels through the building structure itself — floors, walls, and ceilings.

As a renter, you can't rebuild walls or replace floors. But you can:

- **Add mass** to walls using heavy furniture
- **Absorb sound** inside your unit with soft surfaces
- **Seal gaps** where airborne noise leaks in
- **Mask remaining noise** with white noise or background sound

Each section below covers one of these approaches with specific products, Canadian pricing, and installation methods that won't cost you your deposit.

---

## Seal the Gaps First: Weatherstripping and Door Sweeps

The single most effective thing most renters can do is seal the gap under and around their front door. In older Canadian apartments, the gap under the door can be 15mm or more — enough for hallway conversations, cooking smells, and traffic noise from the lobby to come straight in.

### Door sweeps

A removable door sweep slides onto the bottom of the door and peels off when you move out. Look for adhesive-backed sweeps or ones with a tension fit.

- **Canadian Tire** carries basic adhesive door sweeps for $8–$15 CAD
- **Home Depot Canada** stocks adjustable aluminium sweeps from $12–$25 CAD
- **Amazon.ca** has slide-on twin-draft stoppers (the fabric tube kind) from $10–$18 CAD

The twin-draft stoppers are the easiest to install — they slide under the door with no tools and no adhesive. They're less effective than a proper sweep but better than nothing, and they come off in two seconds on move-out day.

### Weatherstripping tape

Self-adhesive foam or rubber weatherstripping seals the gaps around the door frame. It compresses when the door closes, blocking both noise and drafts.

- A roll of **foam weatherstripping tape** costs $5–$12 CAD at most hardware stores
- **V-strip (vinyl)** weatherstripping is slightly more durable and runs $8–$15 CAD
- For windows, use the same foam tape along the frame edges where you feel drafts

Apply weatherstripping around the full door frame — top and both sides. Clean the surface with rubbing alcohol first so the adhesive sticks properly. It peels off cleanly on most painted metal and wood frames.

### Don't forget the windows

Older single-pane windows in Canadian apartments let in a lot of street noise. If your building hasn't upgraded to double-pane, you can:

- Apply **window insulation film** (the shrink-wrap kind from 3M or Frost King, $10–$20 CAD per window kit) — it creates a dead-air buffer that dampens sound and improves insulation for winter
- Use **removable caulk** (rope caulk) around the window frame for $5–$8 CAD per roll
- Add heavy curtains on top of either option (covered below)

---

## Rugs and Underlay: Your Floor Is a Speaker

Hard floors — laminate, vinyl plank, hardwood, concrete — reflect sound instead of absorbing it. Every footstep, chair scrape, and dropped phone echoes around the room and transmits downward to the unit below.

A thick area rug with a dense underlay is one of the highest-impact noise changes you can make.

### What to look for

- **Pile height matters.** A shag or high-pile rug absorbs more sound than a flat-weave kilim. For noise reduction, thicker is better.
- **Underlay is half the job.** A felt or rubber rug pad underneath adds mass and absorbs vibration. An 8mm felt pad runs $40–$80 CAD for a 5×8 foot size at stores like Wayfair.ca or HomeSense.
- **Cover as much floor as possible.** One small rug in the centre of a room won't do much. Ideally, cover at least 60–70% of the hard floor area in rooms where noise is a problem.

### Where to buy in Canada

- **IKEA Canada** — the VINDUM high-pile rug starts around $200 CAD for 170×230cm
- **HomeSense / Winners** — unpredictable stock but regularly has large rugs for $80–$150 CAD
- **Wayfair.ca** — wide selection, frequent sales, filter by pile height
- **Facebook Marketplace** — used rugs in good condition often go for $30–$60 CAD in major cities

If you're in a condo with a noise clause in the bylaws (common in Toronto and Vancouver buildings), rugs with underlay help you stay compliant.

---

## Heavy Curtains for Windows and Doors

Curtains made from dense, heavy fabric absorb sound reflections inside your room and reduce noise coming through windows. They won't block a jackhammer, but they noticeably soften traffic noise, sirens, and street-level conversations.

### What works

- **Thermal blackout curtains** are often heavy enough to double as sound-absorbing curtains. The multi-layer ones (with a foam or felt backing) perform best.
- **Hang them floor to ceiling** and wider than the window frame — an extra 15–20cm on each side. Sound sneaks around the edges of short or narrow curtains.
- **Use a ceiling-mounted curtain rod** or a tension rod for a no-drill option. Tension rods work well in window alcoves and for hanging a curtain across a bedroom doorway.

### Canadian pricing

- IKEA's MAJGULL blackout curtains run about $50–$70 CAD per pair and are heavy enough for decent sound absorption
- Amazon.ca carries "soundproof curtains" (really just heavy blackout curtains with a felt layer) for $40–$90 CAD per panel
- For a doorway curtain to block hallway noise, a heavy blanket on a tension rod works well and costs very little

If you're dealing with both noise and winter cold, heavy curtains solve both problems at once — they reduce drafts and cut heating costs, which matters in a Canadian winter.

---

## Acoustic Panels: What They Do (and Don't Do)

Acoustic panels are the first thing people search for when they want a quieter apartment. It's worth understanding what they actually do before you spend money.

**What they do:** Absorb sound reflections inside your room. If your apartment echoes — voices sound harsh, music sounds muddy, phone calls pick up reverb — acoustic panels fix that by soaking up reflected sound waves.

**What they don't do:** Block sound from coming through a wall. A foam panel on a shared wall will not stop your neighbour's bass, TV, or conversations. Sound transmission through walls requires mass, not absorption.

### Renter-friendly mounting

- **Command strips** (3M) hold lightweight fabric-wrapped panels up to about 3kg per strip set. Use multiple strips per panel.
- **Lean panels against the wall** on a shelf or on the floor, propped at an angle. This works well for large panels and avoids wall contact entirely.
- **Hang from a picture rail** if your apartment has one (common in older Montreal and Toronto buildings).

### Canadian pricing and sources

- **Primacoustic** (Canadian company, based in BC) makes professional-grade panels. Their Broadway series starts around $80–$120 CAD per panel, available through Long & McQuade or Amazon.ca.
- **Amazon.ca** has budget wedge foam panels (12-packs) for $25–$40 CAD — these work for echo reduction but look less polished.
- **DIY option:** Rigid fibreglass insulation (Roxul/Rockwool Safe'n'Sound, about $60 CAD per batt from Home Depot) wrapped in fabric makes an effective panel for half the cost of retail. There are dozens of tutorials online for this. Just wear gloves and a mask when cutting fibreglass.

Place panels at the first reflection points — the walls directly beside and across from where you sit or sleep. Two or three well-placed panels do more than covering an entire wall randomly.

---

## Furniture Placement as Noise Control

Where you put your furniture changes how much noise you hear, and this costs nothing.

### Use bookshelves as sound barriers

A tall, heavy bookshelf — fully loaded with books — against a shared wall adds meaningful mass. Mass is what actually blocks sound transmission. A single Billy bookcase from IKEA ($90–$130 CAD) filled with books provides more sound blocking than a wall full of foam panels.

For maximum effect:

- **Fill every shelf.** Half-empty shelves don't add enough mass.
- **Push the bookcase flush against the wall.** No air gap.
- **Use multiple bookcases** on a long shared wall if you have them.

If you're short on books, thrift stores and library sales in Canadian cities sell hardcovers by the bag. It doesn't matter what the books are — you need the weight.

### Move your bed away from the noisy wall

If your bedroom shares a wall with a neighbour's living room or kitchen, rearrange so your headboard is on the opposite wall. This is especially useful in [condo layouts](/blog/condo-storage-ideas-toronto-vancouver) where bedrooms are stacked next to common areas.

### Upholstered furniture absorbs sound

A fabric sofa absorbs more sound than a leather one. An upholstered headboard absorbs more than a bare wall. If you're choosing between two pieces of furniture and noise is a concern, go with the softer, heavier option.

---

## White Noise and Sound Masking

Some noise can't be blocked — you can reduce it, but a thin wall is still a thin wall. Sound masking fills your space with consistent background noise that makes intermittent sounds (a door slamming, a dog barking, a conversation next door) less noticeable.

### Options

- **White noise machines** — the LectroFan (around $60–$80 CAD on Amazon.ca) is a popular choice with multiple sound profiles. The Yogasleep Dohm (about $55–$70 CAD) uses a real fan inside for a more natural sound.
- **A regular fan** works if you're not picky about the sound profile. Box fans and tower fans from Canadian Tire ($25–$50 CAD) produce enough ambient noise to mask hallway and street sounds.
- **Apps and smart speakers** — free white noise apps (myNoise, White Noise Lite) or asking your Google/Alexa device to play brown noise cost nothing.

White noise is especially helpful for sleep. If you work from home in a noisy apartment, noise-cancelling headphones (starting around $80 CAD for decent over-ear models) are worth the investment, but that's personal audio, not room treatment.

---

## Provincial Noise Bylaws: What the Law Says

Every Canadian province handles noise complaints differently, and the specifics depend on your municipality. Here's a general overview — always check your own city's bylaw for exact hours and enforcement.

| Province / City | Typical quiet hours | Who enforces |
|---|---|---|
| Ontario (Toronto) | 11 PM – 7 AM (city bylaw) | Municipal bylaw officers |
| Quebec (Montreal) | 9 PM – 7 AM weekdays, 9 PM – 9 AM weekends (varies by borough) | Ville de Montréal, police for extreme cases |
| BC (Vancouver) | 10 PM – 7 AM | City bylaw officers |
| Alberta (Calgary) | 10 PM – 7 AM | Community peace officers |
| Alberta (Edmonton) | 10 PM – 7 AM | Bylaw enforcement |

A few things to keep in mind:

- **Your lease may have stricter rules.** Many condo boards and property managers set quiet hours earlier than the municipal bylaw.
- **Bylaws typically cover "unreasonable" noise**, not all noise. Normal living sounds (walking, talking at a normal volume, running appliances) are generally not bylaw violations, even if you can hear them.
- **Document before you complain.** If a neighbour's noise is genuinely excessive, keep a log of dates, times, and descriptions before contacting your landlord or filing a complaint. In Ontario, the Landlord and Tenant Board handles disputes between tenants and landlords; in Quebec, it's the Tribunal administratif du logement.

Knowing your rights matters, but the practical reality is that most apartment noise comes down to building construction. The strategies above help you control your own environment regardless of what's happening next door.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Priority Order

If you're starting from scratch and want the most noise reduction for the least money and effort, work through this list in order:

1. **Seal the front door** — weatherstripping tape and a door sweep ($15–$25 CAD total)
2. **Add a thick rug with underlay** to the loudest room ($80–$200 CAD depending on source)
3. **Hang heavy curtains** on windows facing the street ($50–$100 CAD per window)
4. **Push a loaded bookshelf** against the noisiest shared wall (free if you already own one)
5. **Add 2–3 acoustic panels** at reflection points if echo is a problem ($50–$120 CAD)
6. **Use a white noise machine** for sleep or focused work ($30–$80 CAD)

For renters following our [no-damage decor guide](/blog/renters-no-damage-decor-guide-canada), every item on this list uses removable mounting or freestanding placement. Nothing here requires landlord permission in any Canadian province.

The total cost to meaningfully quiet a one-bedroom apartment is roughly $200–$500 CAD if you're buying new. If you source rugs and bookshelves secondhand, you can do it for well under $150 CAD.

---

## Platform Bed With Storage: Best Options in Canada

URL: https://smallspacehome.ca/blog/platform-bed-with-storage-canada/

The bedroom in a small Canadian apartment almost always has the same problem: the closet is too small, there is no storage dresser because there is no room for one, and the floor under the bed is either wasted or filled with mismatched bins that slide around and collect dust.

A platform bed with built-in storage solves all three issues at once. It converts dead under-bed space into organized storage, keeps the bedroom floor clear, and eliminates the need for a freestanding dresser in many apartments. This guide covers what is actually available in Canada in 2026, what each type holds, and how to choose.

---

## Two Types of Storage Platform Beds

### Drawer beds

Pull-out drawers are built into one or both sides of the platform base. Most queen beds come with 2 drawers (one per side); some models offer 4. The drawers typically do not have full extension, meaning they pull out about 60–70% of their depth before stopping — planned storage works better than ad hoc use.

**What fits:** Folded clothing, bedding, seasonal items, shoes (lying flat), craft supplies, extra towels. Drawers work well for anything you access 1–3 times a week.

**What does not fit:** Suitcases, large duvets, bulky winter gear. The drawer height is typically 18–22 cm — a rolling suitcase does not fit.

**Clearance:** Drawer beds need about 60 cm of free space on each side of the bed for the drawers to open fully. In a small bedroom, this is often the limiting factor.

### Hydraulic lift beds

The entire platform (with mattress) lifts up on gas struts, revealing a large open cavity that runs the full length and width of the bed. There are no side clearance requirements — the storage is accessed from the foot or side by lifting the mattress.

**What fits:** Everything a drawer bed cannot. Full suitcases, large duvets and comforters still in their storage bags, seasonal clothing in bins, athletic gear, extra bedding sets, books, electronics in boxes.

**Capacity:** A queen lift bed holds approximately 400–600 litres. That is the equivalent of 3–4 large IKEA SAMLA bins (55 L each) laid flat, or a full wardrobe of off-season clothing plus a suitcase.

**Trade-off:** You must get off the mattress to access storage. The mechanism is strong — gas struts hold the platform fully open with no effort — but it is not a quick grab like a drawer. Best for items you access monthly, not daily.

---

## Platform Storage Beds Available in Canada

### IKEA SLATTUM (drawer bed)

**Price:** ~$350–$450 CAD (queen)
**Storage:** 2 pull-out drawers, one per side, no lid — open top storage
**Height:** 43 cm from floor to top of frame

The SLATTUM is IKEA's entry-level upholstered drawer bed. The drawers are open-top (no drawer front cover), so they work as open bins rather than closed drawers — fine for folded bedding, less good for loose small items. Frame is fabric-upholstered over engineered wood. Available in a few neutral colours. Ships to most Canadian addresses, available for pickup or delivery at IKEA Canada locations.

Best for: Budget-conscious renters who primarily need off-season bedding and clothing storage.

### IKEA NORDLI (drawer bed)

**Price:** ~$500–$700 CAD (queen, depends on configuration)
**Storage:** Modular — 2, 4, or 6 drawers depending on configuration
**Height:** 38 cm

The NORDLI is IKEA's most flexible storage bed. The modular system lets you configure more drawers on one side than the other, add a headboard with charging ports, and customize width. White only (as of 2026). Drawers are covered with the same white finish — cleaner look than the SLATTUM. The soft-close mechanism on higher-end configurations is good but not as smooth as purpose-built bedroom furniture.

Best for: Maximising drawer storage in a studio or one-bedroom apartment where the drawer configuration can be matched to available room layout.

### IKEA BRIMNES (drawer bed)

**Price:** ~$450–$550 CAD (queen)
**Storage:** 4 drawers (2 per side), closed-front
**Height:** 47 cm

The BRIMNES is IKEA's four-drawer option. Closed-front drawers look like proper furniture rather than open bins. The headboard has two small shelves built in, adding nightstand-equivalent storage. White or black finish. One of the most widely owned beds in Canadian apartments due to the four-drawer layout — doubles the storage of most drawer beds at nearly the same price point.

Best for: Anyone who wants to use the storage bed as a dresser replacement, eliminating the need for a separate chest of drawers in a small bedroom.

### Zinus Upholstered Platform Bed with Storage (drawer bed)

**Price:** ~$400–$600 CAD (queen, Amazon.ca)
**Storage:** 2 or 4 drawers depending on model
**Height:** 45–50 cm

> **Our top pick:** This [upholstered platform bed with 2 storage drawers](https://www.amazon.ca/dp/B0DZ2ZDXKM?tag=smallspace06f-20) (~$240 CAD) is the most-reviewed storage bed on Amazon.ca Canada — fabric upholstered, easy assembly, 2 side drawers.

Zinus is one of the most reviewed mattress and bed frame brands on Amazon.ca. Their storage beds are available in queen and king, upholstered in light grey, beige, or dark grey fabric. Assembly is straightforward. The drawers are side-slide with a stopper (no full extension). Build quality is good for the price — the frame is heavy engineered wood over a steel grid, which is more rigid than pure MDF construction.

Best for: Renters who want a complete packaged look (upholstered, no visible wood grain) without IKEA's assembly complexity.

### Wayfair Canada: Hydraulic Lift Options

Wayfair Canada carries the largest selection of hydraulic lift beds available to Canadian buyers. Price range for a queen lift bed: **$600–$1,200 CAD**, with the most common models landing around $700–$900.

**What to look for on Wayfair:**

- **Gas strut rating**: Should be listed — look for 1,500 N or higher. Lower-rated struts struggle with a full mattress.
- **Base material**: Solid wood slats or a steel grid hold the mattress better than thin MDF panels, which can bow over time.
- **Access point**: Foot-of-bed lift vs. side lift. Foot lift requires more floor space at the end of the bed (50+ cm) but does not require clearance on the sides.

**Notable models:**

- **Lark Manor Alayah Upholstered Storage Bed** (~$750–$900, queen): Consistent reviews on Wayfair Canada. Linen upholstery, hydraulic lift from the foot end, good cavity depth for suitcases.
- **Winston Porter and George Oliver brands** on Wayfair: Frequently on sale. Build quality ranges widely — read the 1-star reviews specifically for frame cracking or strut failure reports before buying.

Best for: Renters who need maximum storage capacity and are willing to plan access (not grabbing items daily) in exchange for large volume.

### Amazon.ca: Molblly and Giantex Lift Beds

Two brands consistently available on Amazon.ca with good shipping to major Canadian cities:

**Molblly Storage Platform Bed** (~$500–$700, queen): Hydraulic lift, upholstered in grey or beige fabric, free shipping to most provinces. Reviews are strong for the gas strut durability specifically — a common failure point on cheaper lift beds.

**Giantex Platform Bed with Storage** (~$400–$600, queen): Budget lift bed with solid reviews. Assembly instructions are less clear than Zinus or IKEA equivalents, so budget extra time. Ships from Canadian warehouses in most cases — important for avoiding duties.

---

## What to Measure Before Buying

### Bedroom clearance

| Bed type | Side clearance needed | End clearance needed |
|---|---|---|
| Drawer bed (2-drawer) | 60 cm per drawer side | 60 cm minimum |
| Drawer bed (4-drawer) | 60 cm both sides | 60 cm minimum |
| Hydraulic lift (foot-lift) | 50 cm both sides | 80+ cm |
| Hydraulic lift (side-lift) | 80+ cm one side | 50 cm minimum |

In a small apartment bedroom (typically 3 × 3.5 m or 3 × 4 m), a 4-drawer queen bed often cannot open all four drawers — the side with the closet or wall does not have 60 cm. Check your actual clearance before choosing a 4-drawer over 2-drawer.

### Ceiling and loft clearance

Platform storage beds sit higher than basic frames. A hydraulic lift bed with a 30 cm mattress on a 50 cm base sits about 80 cm off the floor — not unusual, but something to verify in apartments with low-profile furniture or low ceilings.

### Door width

All storage beds ship disassembled. The longest single piece in a queen storage bed frame is typically 215 cm (the side rail). Standard Canadian apartment exterior doors are 81 cm wide; interior doors are 76–81 cm. A 215 cm rail at any angle passes through an 81 cm doorway — no issue.

---

## Storage Bed vs. Separate Under-Bed Storage

If the bed you have is already good and replacing it is not practical, standalone under-bed storage is the alternative.

**Under-bed storage bins** (IKEA SKUBB or similar, ~$15–$30 for 2): Work on beds with 20+ cm of floor clearance. Flat bins for clothing and bedding; rolling bins for heavier items. The problem is access — bins slide to the back and are inconvenient to retrieve from.

**Under-bed storage drawers on wheels** (Amazon.ca, ~$40–$80): Freestanding rolling drawers that live under a platform bed with adequate clearance. Easier access than flat bins. Limited capacity — typically 2 drawers, each 15 cm deep.

**Storage bed verdict:** If you plan to stay in the apartment 12+ months and the bedroom has adequate clearance, a storage bed pays for itself in cabinet space freed. If you move frequently or the bedroom is very narrow, bins under the current bed are the practical choice.

For more options on extracting value from under-bed space, see [under-bed storage ideas for small apartments](/blog/under-bed-storage-ideas-small-apartment). For the full bedroom storage picture including closets and vertical space, [small apartment bedroom storage ideas](/blog/small-apartment-bedroom-storage-ideas) covers every zone.

---

|---|---|---|---|
| IKEA SLATTUM | Drawer | 2 drawers | ~$350–$450 |
| IKEA BRIMNES | Drawer | 4 drawers | ~$450–$550 |
